rows.grounds: bhāva = entity/being; artha-prakāśa = manifestation of objects; ātmā = nature; compound describing knowledge
eka = single; vijñātṛ = knower; vedyatva = knowability

items.question: If knowledge manifests objects, can something known by one knower be known by another?
premises: Knowledge has the nature of manifesting objects.
If knowability belonged only to a single knower, that knowledge would be unreal for others.
Knowability by a single knower excludes knowability by another knower.
items.inference: Restricting knowability to one knower makes shared knowledge impossible and undermines the reality of knowledge.
uncertainties: The exact referent of 'this knowledge' is context-dependent.
items.plain_english: Knowledge is by nature the manifestation of objects. But if something were knowable only by a single knower, that knowledge would be unreal, because what is knowable by one knower would not be knowable by another.

rows.grounds: samasta = all; jñātṛ = knower; vedyatva = knowability
na = not; eka = single; vijñātṛ = knower; vedyatā = knowability
bhāva = entity; dharma = property/nature; asti = is

items.question: Can knowability be a property belonging to an entity itself?
premises: If knowability belonged to all knowers, it could not belong to a single knower as such.
Knowability cannot be consistently assigned either to one knower or to all knowers as an entity's property.
A property that cannot be coherently located is not a property of the entity.
items.inference: Knowability is not any property inherent in an entity.
items.plain_english: If something were knowable by all knowers, it would not be knowable by a single knower in that exclusive sense. Therefore, knowability is not any property that belongs to an entity.

rows.grounds: artha = object; grahaṇa = grasping; rūpa = form

items.question: What is the knowability of an entity if it is not an inherent property?
premises: Knowability cannot be an inherent property of an entity.
Consciousness arises in the form of grasping an object.
This arising of consciousness occurs within consciousness itself.
items.inference: The knowability of an entity is nothing other than the arising of consciousness in the form of object-grasping.
items.plain_english: The knowability of an entity is that very arising of consciousness which takes the form of grasping an object, occurring within consciousness itself.

rows.grounds: prakāśya = to be manifested; artha = object; tam = that
prati = toward; eṣā = this; eva = very

items.question: How should knowability be understood in relation to manifest objects?
premises: A manifest object comes together with consciousness in the act of knowing.
This convergence toward the object is what is called knowability.
Knowability is therefore not a separate property residing in objects.
items.inference: Knowability is the event of consciousness converging on a manifest object, not a property of objects.
uncertainties: The sandhi in 'prakāśyo@rthastaṃ' allows slight variation in parsing.
items.plain_english: When a manifest object comes together with consciousness, that very convergence toward it is knowability. Here we say that knowability is not a property of objects.

rows.grounds: syuḥ = they would be; jñāne = in knowledge
pṛthu-budhna = broad base; ādi = and so on; rūpa = form

items.question: What follows if knowability were treated as a property of objects?
premises: If knowability were an object's property, objects would remain unknowable even when described in knowledge.
A pot may have features like a broad base.
The mere presence of such features does not make another thing share them.
items.inference: Treating knowability as an object-property fails to explain how objects become known.
items.plain_english: If knowability were a property of objects, they would remain unknowable even when described in knowledge. Just as a pot may have a broad base and other features, that alone does not make something else take on those features.

rows.grounds: pṛthu-budhna-ādi-rūpa = form of broad base etc.; -tā = state

items.question: Why does the presence of knowledge not make objects inherently knowable?
premises: A cloth does not acquire the form of a pot even when the pot's features exist.
Knowledge inheres in the knower, not in external objects.
An object does not take on a nature that belongs elsewhere.
items.inference: Even when knowledge is present in the knower, objects do not thereby possess knowability as their own nature.
items.plain_english: A cloth does not take on the form of a pot with a broad base and so on. In the same way, even when knowledge is present in the knower, objects do not thereby become knowable by their own nature.
